title: Raise the cutoff. Who slips through?
hook: A test scores everyone, then draws a line. The line decides which mistake you make.

knows: false positives matter when a condition is rare (base-rates)
doesNotKnow: that moving a cutoff trades false alarms for misses
that only a better test shrinks both

misconception: A stricter cutoff makes a test better: it can have no false alarms and no missed cases at once.
objective: The learner can say that raising the cutoff cuts false alarms but misses more sick people (and the reverse), and that only separating the two score curves shrinks both errors.
keyState: Cutoff raised to 1.5 (31% missed, 6.7% false alarms) and lowered to 0.5 (6.7% missed, 31% false alarms), then the better test shown.

claims.text: In the toy model healthy people score about 0 and sick people about 2, both with spread 1 (a normal curve).
claims.source: Toy model stated on the stage and in the question; it is not a real clinical test. Constants SICK, BETTER in src/demos/probability/sliding-the-cutoff/model.ts.

claims.text: With the cutoff at 1, 15.9% of sick people are missed and 15.9% of healthy people are falsely flagged.
claims.source: missed = Phi(1 - 2) = Phi(-1) = 0.1587; false alarms = 1 - Phi(1) = 0.1587 (normal table; errors() in model.ts).

claims.text: Raising the cutoff to 1.5 misses 30.9% of sick people and falsely flags 6.7% of healthy people.
claims.source: Phi(-0.5) = 0.3085; 1 - Phi(1.5) = 0.0668 (normal table; recomputed in node from errors()).

claims.text: Lowering the cutoff to 0.5 misses 6.7% of sick people and falsely flags 30.9% of healthy people.
A better test, with the sick scores centred at 3 instead of 2, misses fewer sick people at the same cutoff with the same false alarms; at 1.5 both errors are 6.7%.
claims.source: Phi(c - 3) < Phi(c - 2) for every cutoff c, while false alarms depend only on the healthy curve and c; at c = 1.5 both errors are 1 - Phi(1.5) = 6.7% (computed from errors(1.5, 3)).

claims.text: Moving the cutoff trades one mistake for the other: missed rises as false alarms fall.
claims.source: missed = Phi(c - 2) increases in c; false alarms = 1 - Phi(c) decreases in c.

recall.question: A screening test flags everyone whose score is above a line. You move the line so fewer healthy people are flagged. What happens to the sick people the test misses?
options: No change, the test is the same
recall.why: The curves overlap, so a higher line cuts false alarms but leaves more sick scores below it. Only a test whose curves overlap less improves both.
